title: DYNAMICS OF PORTFOLIO ASSESSMENT STRATEGY IN EVALUATING THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE SKILLS FOR PUPILS WITH HEARING IMPAIRMENTS IN FAKO DIVISION, SOUTH WEST REGION OF CAMEROON
authors: Ngenwie Emilia Tanyie; Therese Mungah Shalo Tchombe
venue: International Journal of Developmental Issues in Education and Humanities
abstract: This study examined the impact of portfolio assessment on evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment in Fako Division, Cameroon. Portfolio assessment, as an informal and learner-centred approach, was explored within the framework of inclusive education, where traditional assessment methods often fail to adequately reflect the abilities of learners with hearing loss. The research utilised a quasi-experimental design involving pupils with hearing impairment in selected inclusive primary schools. Data were gathered through English language tests, classroom observations, and interviews with parents, teachers, head teachers, and the divisional delegate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, and regression analysis, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. The results indicated that pupils subjected to portfolio assessment performed significantly better in English language skills than those assessed through conventional methods. Statistical analysis (SPSS t-tests and regression) showed that pupils assessed via portfolios scored notably higher on post-tests (portfolio group mean=12.78 versus control=11.14; t(38)=2.919, p<.05). Regression analysis demonstrated that portfolio use was a strong predictor of language improvement (β=0.336, p<.001). Classroom observations and interview findings further revealed that portfolio assessment encouraged ongoing learning, increased learner engagement, self-reflection, and heightened teacher awareness of individual progress. The study concludes that portfolio assessment is an effective method for evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment and recommends its systematic adoption within inclusive classroom practice.

title: From Embedded Finance to Embedded Obligation: A Law-and-Economics Theory of Consumer Protection in Platform-Mediated Financial Services
authors: Yongxin Chen
abstract: Embedded finance is usually described as the integration of financial services into non-financial platforms. This article argues that the deeper regulatory transformation is the embedding of future legal and economic obligations into ordinary consumption, work, business, and entertainment environments. When credit, payment, wage-advance, wallet, and merchant-financing functions are delivered through plat form architecture, consumer protection cannot focus only on the formal product or licensed provider. It must also examine how obligations are framed, made salient or obscure, personalized through data, and allocated across platforms, merchants, lenders, and technical intermediaries. The article develops a law and-economics theory of Embedded Obligation Architecture, explains its irreducible object, refines its four layers, and distinguishes it from choice architecture, digital nudging, dark patterns, behavioral contract theory, and platform governance. It specifies the evidentiary limits of transferring behavioral evidence to embedded-finance contexts and proposes a Functional Embedded Obligation Test as a standard with gateway elements, evidentiary thresholds, legal vehicles, safe harbors, and proportionate remedies.

title: The Sociolinguistics of Machine Identity: LLM Personality and Ideology Propagation
authors: Guangni Li
abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) possess a measurable "personality," and how do the linguistic properties of training corpora shape their cognitive style and downstream reasoning? This paper approaches these questions from a sociolinguistic perspective on machine "identity." This manuscript is positioned explicitly as a conceptual perspective paper: it does not present original experimental data, nor does it constitute a systematic review with defined search strategies or inclusion criteria. Instead, it synthesises key published findings into two original theoretical frameworks intended to guide future empirical and engineering work. We examine evidence that LLMs exhibit reliable, valid Big Five personality traits—particularly in large, instruction-tuned models—and that continued pre-training on domain-specific corpora may shape those traits through measurable linguistic features: imperative ratio, type-token ratio (TTR), and syntactic complexity. We then analyse how standard-language ideology embedded in training corpora is amplified in model outputs, disadvantaging dialect and minority-language communities. Building on these findings, we propose two conceptual contributions: (1) a Personality Engineering (PE) framework for targeted continued pre-training to cultivate task-appropriate cognitive profiles, and (2) a Language Ideology Propagation Model (LIPM) mapping the pipeline from corpus composition to societal impact. Both frameworks are explicitly conceptual and require empirical validation before they can function as operational guidelines. Their value lies in structuring future research and providing a shared vocabulary for cross-disciplinary collaboration, with direct implications for responsible AI deployment.
keywords: semantic communication; semantic encoding; semantic channel coding

title: From Legal Databases to AI-Assisted Justice: A Risk-Sensitive Framework for the Application of Information Technologies in Law
authors: Li Yongxin
abstract: This paper analyzes information technologies in law and proposes a risk-sensitive framework for responsible digital legal practice. Using EU regulatory developments as the main legal lens, while also referring to international standards and policy materials, the study reviews legal databases, case-management systems, artificial intelligence and natural language processing, electronic identification and signatures, digital evidence, online dispute resolution and electronic courts. The paper's contribution is to connect general principles of transparency, human oversight, source verification and accountability to concrete stages of legal work: intake, research, drafting, identity assurance, signing, archiving and audit. Brief examples of AI-assisted drafting, online dispute resolution and electronic signature verification illustrate the practical use of the framework. The analysis concludes that digital legal systems create value when they remain traceable, proportionate and subject to professional responsibility rather than replacing legal judgment.
keywords: semantic communication; semantic communications; semantic-aware communication

title: Measuring Activity-Space Segregation with Multi-Source Big Data: A Physical--Digital Framework with Simulation Validation and a Real-Data Proof of Concept
authors: Guangwei Wang
abstract: Segregation research increasingly measures who people encounter beyond home, yet physical mobility, place semantics, and digital activity are often combined without clear construct boundaries. This study develops a physical--digital activity-space framework that distinguishes co-presence, digital exposure, and digital interaction, and represents physical and digital segregation as separate components rather than a forced composite. Validation is deliberately split by evidentiary role. A public Washington--Baltimore Foursquare check-in subset tests the computational feasibility and robustness of a discrete group co-visitation statistic; it does not validate continuous socioeconomic exposure because the dataset lacks individual socioeconomic status. Monte Carlo experiments separately test layer-selective construct response and sensitivity to trace missingness, spatial aggregation, socioeconomic measurement error, and cross-layer coupling. The results show that the proposed calculations are executable and that the synthetic physical and digital components respond selectively to their generating mechanisms, while also revealing important measurement attenuation. No real-data estimate of income segregation, digital exposure, physical--digital coupling, or the causal effect of inequality is reported. The framework therefore combines bounded validation with a falsifiable comparative and causal research agenda.

title: From Chopin to Kitsch? Pauline Viardot's Vocal Mazurkas and the popularisation of classical music
authors: Stacy Olive Jarvis
venue: Journal of Music Theory and Transcultural Music Studies
abstract: This article examines the concept of ‘popular music’ in the context of the work of Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849). The paper analyses six mazurkas by the Polish composer and their transcription for voice and piano, performed by the opera diva Pauline Viardot (1821–1910) to words by the French poet Louis Pomme (1831–1901). This chamber vocal cycle, composed by Viardot, illustrates the established poetics of the salons of the second third of the 19th century, where literature and music converged. Based on an analysis of various sources, this study examines the history of the works’ creation, their imagery and intonation, as well as the harmonic features of these vocal miniatures, whilst reconstructing their context. As a result, a connection is revealed between Viardot’s vocal mazurkas and Chopin’s songs, composed between 1829 and 1847, in the themes of love and loneliness. The aim of this article is to investigate how the opera singer bridges the gap between classical music and the mass audience and becomes a creator of kitsch. The research methodology includes an analysis of historical sources, as well as a musical and literary analysis of Chopin’s and Viardot’s mazurkas. The author concludes that kitsch emerges at the intersection of classical and popular music, where the integration of various elements from different mazurkas helps Viardot achieve a precise correspondence between the expressive content of the text and Chopin’s musical language.

title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
authors: Hanna David
venue: Journal of Child Development, Exceptionality and Education
abstract: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent games and serious real-world aggression remains more contested, with recent research emphasizing relatively small effects and the importance of individual and contextual factors. Overall, the evidence suggests that the developmental consequences of gaming for children and adolescents depend less on gaming itself than on the duration, content, context, and pattern of engagement.

title: Triage models for surgical decision-making in patients with shoulder pain: an integrative review.
authors: Samah Hassan; Kenneth J Faber; Joy Christine MacDermid
abstract: Shoulder pain is a major cause of work absenteeism, affecting 1 in 3 adults. Although nonsurgical treatments like physical therapy are recommended as the first line of management, 40% of patients are referred for surgery before exploring these options. This review aimed to identify existing triage models used for shoulder pain referrals for surgery, guidelines for shoulder pain management that include criteria for surgical referral, and indications for surgery. An integrative review approach was used to comprehensively search major databases (Medline, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL Plus) and gray literature. Articles on triage models, referral processes, or surgery candidacy for shoulder pain were included. The searches retrieved 4510 articles, with 480 selected for full review and 71 articles included in this synthesis. Thirty-seven articles described various triage models and clinical decision-making processes for managing shoulder pain, including determining when to refer for surgical consultation and the indications for surgery. Seventeen articles compared surgical and nonsurgical treatments to identify surgical indicators, 10 articles examined factors affecting decision-making, and 7 articles explored predictor models for surgical outcomes. The findings underscore the need for a multifactorial decision-making process that acknowledges the complexity of pain within a biopsychosocial framework and incorporates patients' personal preferences into the triage decision-making process. These triage models should work across different contexts, eg, conservative, primary, and speciality care, to facilitate better patient experience across the continuum.

title: The Impact of Business Environmental Changes on the Adoption of a Strategic Pivot: A Case Study of Zar Industrial Group
authors: Alireza Mansourkhaki; Kambiz Talebi; Jahangir Yadollahi Farsi
venue: International Journal of Innovation Management and Organizational Behavior (IJIMOB)
abstract: Objective: This study aimed to examine the impact of business environmental changes on strategic pivot adoption in Zar Industrial Group and develop a conceptual model of this process. Methods and Materials: This applied qualitative study used a grounded theory design. The study population consisted of Zar Industrial Group managers and university professors with expertise in strategic management and organizational change. Participants were selected purposively based on their knowledge and professional experience. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with managers of the holding company and its food-industry subsidiaries, together with academic experts. Interviews continued until theoretical saturation, resulting in a final sample of 12 participants. Interview transcripts were systematically coded, compared, and categorized to identify the principal dimensions and mechanisms associated with strategic pivot adoption. Findings: The analysis produced seven main categories and 41 related concepts. The categories included macro-environmental changes and external pressures; risk, uncertainty, and financial pressure; supply-chain and operational disruptions; market-oriented and commercial responses; structural and business-model redesign; innovation, technology, and digital transformation; and human capital, organizational learning, and institutionalization of the strategic pivot. Environmental turbulence generated financial, operational, and market pressures that stimulated coordinated strategic responses. These responses involved market reorientation, business-model redesign, technological innovation, digital transformation, and capability development. Human capital and organizational learning played a central role in sustaining and institutionalizing the strategic pivot. Conclusion: Strategic pivot adoption in Zar Industrial Group represents a multidimensional organizational response to environmental uncertainty rather than an isolated managerial decision. Successful pivots require alignment among market responses, structural transformation, technological innovation, operational resilience, and organizational learning. The proposed conceptual model can help managers recognize environmental signals, coordinate adaptive actions, and strengthen organizational resilience and long-term competitiveness.

title: Designing an Educational Planning Model Based on the Agricultural Value Chain with a Qualitative Approach
authors: Bentolhoda Ramezanzadeh; Hamidreza Arasteh; Kamran Mohammadkhani; Abbasali Motalebi
venue: Future of Work and Digital Management Journal
abstract: Educational planning based on the agricultural value chain, as a comprehensive and systematic approach, can make a substantial contribution to improving quality and productivity in the agricultural sector. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to design an educational planning model based on the agricultural value chain in citrus orchards in northern Iran. This study is classified as qualitative grounded-theory research. The statistical population consisted of 20 experts and faculty members of the Agricultural Research, Education and Extension Organization. Interviews were used for data collection, and MAXQDA 2020 software was employed for data analysis. The findings identified the research components, including causal conditions consisting of core content, educational activities, and supplementary programs; the central phenomenon, namely educational programs based on the agricultural value chain; contextual factors including macro-level policies and culture; intervening factors including evaluation, core policies, competition, and educational approaches; strategies including organizational strategies and environmental strategies; and outcomes including optimal value chain management, quality orientation, and educational enhancement.

title: Vision--RF Cooperative ISAC for Dynamic V2I Networks: Adaptive Beam Management and Semantic Clutter Suppression
authors: Wenqi~Fan; Ning~Wei; Xiangyu Dong; Ahmad~Bazzi; Guan Gui; Rongyan~Xi; Huimin Tang; Yue~Xiu
abstract: We develop a vision--radio-frequency (RF) cooperative integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) framework that jointly uses visual priors and RF observations for transmit-side beam control and receiver-side clutter suppression. Within a narrowband snapshot model, visual target priors and historical RF detections guide control in dynamic vehicle-to-infrastructure networks with roadside clutter. In this framework, posterior angular uncertainty determines beam control and the selection between communication-for-sensing and sensing-for-sensing modes. To reduce sensing overhead while accommodating unreliable visual information, we develop a reliability-adaptive beam scanning scheme that allocates a bounded scan budget according to visual target probabilities and RF history, while reserving an adaptive fraction for exploration. At the receiver, visual geometry identifies clutter support, and RF observations estimate the corresponding complex reflection coefficients. Motion-aware residual filtering is then applied before angle--Doppler detection to suppress clutter while preserving slow-moving targets. Furthermore, communication and sensing power allocation is formulated as a per-direction linear program, subject to signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio constraints evaluated at angles sampled from the posterior distribution and a total-power budget. Simulation results show that the proposed framework improves tracking over static and vision-only beam control and reduces sensing overhead relative to full scanning. The proposed scanning scheme also provides greater robustness to visual blockage than fixed-weight scanning, while the receiver better preserves slow-moving targets than temporal cancellation when visual target information is available.

title: Mobile Embodied Agent Network (MEAN): Integrated Framework, Enabling Technologies, and Task-Driven Deployment
authors: Zhaoyang Zhang; Lingxiao Sun; Weijie Zhou; Chunhui Feng; Zhaohui Yang; Xuan Cheng; Tianyi Qin; Zhixian Kong; Baoping Cheng; Zijian Wu; Jingze Che
abstract: Mobile networks are evolving from human-centered, data-oriented communication infrastructures toward machine- and/or agent-dominant, task-oriented platforms that are to serve the rapidly increasing networked machines and embodied agents. In order to fulfill the newly arose complex task objectives, the framework of future mobile network is to be innovated to reflect and facilitate the intrinsic interplay and integration of the underlying processes of perception, communication, computation, decision, action, and feedback, etc. This survey establishes the mobile embodied agent network (MEAN) as a task-oriented networking paradigm in which networking and distributed intelligence are jointly organized around closed-loop embodied task execution. We first establish a unified MEAN framework that explains how network resources and intelligent functions jointly support embodied task execution, and extend its performance indicators from conventional communication metrics to embodied task outcomes and cross-layer system effects. With this framework, we analyze three complementary enabling mechanisms that form a cognition-interaction-adaption loop. Large artificial intelligence (AI) models provide high-level cognition, token communication connects this cognition with distributed agents through shared semantic representations, and reinforcement learning closes the loop by adapting system operation to network, task, and physical feedback. We further investigate the bidirectional interplay between MEAN and emerging technologies, showing how they mutually extend system capabilities and reshape task-oriented network design. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future research directions toward the practical realization of MEAN over real joint communication and computation platform.

title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
authors: Masashi Aono
abstract: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.

title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
authors: Tyler Bonnet; Marek Rei
abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.

title: Image CL-SEC: Cross-Layer Semantic Error Correction for Image Communication
authors: Feifan Zhang; Xuelin Bai; Yirun Wang; Yuyang Du; Soung Chang Liew
abstract: Semantic error correction (SEC) uses the semantic knowledge of pretrained models to complement conventional channel decoding. By combining physical-layer decoding information with application-layer semantic predictions, cross-layer SEC (CL-SEC) has demonstrated substantial performance gains in text transmission; however, its applicability to image transmission remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes Image CL-SEC, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first extension of the CL-SEC framework to image transmission. Image CL-SEC uses channel-decoding information together with contextual predictions from a pretrained visual model to resolve residual uncertainty after forward error correction (FEC) decoding. In our implementation, images are represented as discrete visual tokens. For each token position selected for re-evaluation, the probability distribution produced by the channel decoder is combined with the distribution predicted by the visual model to identify the most likely transmitted token. The resulting decision therefore reflects both channel evidence and visual context. Experiments across multiple channel conditions show that, at low and moderate signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), Image CL-SEC improves pixel-level fidelity, perceptual similarity, and token-recovery accuracy relative to either channel decoding or visual-model inference alone. Supplementary experiments using different pretrained visual models further demonstrate that these gains are not specific to a single model.

title: Weakly Supervised Adaptation of Scientific Embeddings for Exploratory Literature Mapping
authors: Roman Neruda; Petra Vidnerová; Jiří Šejnoha; Jakub Mihálik; Tomáš Marvan
abstract: Scientific document embeddings such as SPECTER2 are optimized for retrieval over large, heterogeneous corpora. On a small specialized corpus their similarity distributions can become highly compressed, which limits their usefulness for exploratory literature mapping. We study whether weakly supervised in-domain adaptation, using only metadata already available in open citation databases, changes this geometry. On ArtCon, a curated corpus of 704 publications on artificial and machine consciousness, we adapt the SPECTER2 proximity model with a lightweight LoRA adapter trained on positive pairs derived from bibliographic coupling in OpenAlex, using no manually annotated similarity labels. We compare the adapted embeddings with lexical (TF-IDF), citation-based (bibliographic coupling) and generic semantic (SPECTER2) representations under thresholded, fixed-density and symmetric k-nearest-neighbour graph constructions. Adaptation substantially decompresses the similarity distribution (mean pairwise cosine similarity 0.9104 to 0.8663, standard deviation 0.0259 to 0.0594) and yields graphs with markedly higher Louvain modularity and better connectivity than the base encoder under matched edge and neighbourhood budgets. The effect is stable across all three graph constructions and is therefore not an artefact of a single sparsification choice. We report this as a case study on one corpus, and we are explicit about what it does not establish: the clustering indices used here are computed against community labels derived from each representation's own similarity graph, so they measure internal geometric self-consistency rather than agreement with an external topical ground truth, and adaptation and evaluation use the same documents. Evaluation against independent labels, on held-out documents, and against geometric controls is ongoing work.

title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
authors: Donggyu Yoon; Minsung Hwang; Juneha Baek; Donghyuk Shin; Joyce Jiyoung Whang
abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. To this end, we introduce new benchmark datasets constructed from CIKM, KDD, and SIGIR conference papers, with varied prediction settings, including impact forecasting for emerging concepts unseen during training. We propose MiroGraph, a Multi-agent reasoning framework with scientific concept Graphs, in which a feature designer agent designs predictive features for a given concept pair from structural, semantic, and trend perspectives, and then three LLM agents compute the actual feature values from the enclosing subgraph of the concept pair. Using these feature values, a classifier designer agent constructs a classifier that predicts the final impact labels. MiroGraph outperforms various impact forecasting and temporal link prediction methods.

title: SemVideoSte: Agentic AI for Cross-Modal Semantic Video Steganography Communication
authors: Rui Meng; Song Gao; Tingting Zhu; Zixun Tang; Jinke Ren; Xiaodong Xu; Pei Xiao; Shuguang Cui; Ping Zhang
abstract: We propose an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cross-modal semantic video steganography communication (SemVideoSte) scheme for secure cross-modal information transmission. Agentic AI interprets the service context to determine a semantically matched public prompt and coordinates video generation, message embedding, semantic transmission, and message recovery process. A multi-mask mechanism combines variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction robustness, semantic transmission robustness, and latent separability to select reliable embedding positions. Meanwhile, a private digital token controls the random seed and guidance offset to construct positive and negative terminal latent states, enabling coverless message embedding during the final diffusion sampling step. Simulation results on open-source datasets demonstrate that SemVideoSte achieves high embedding capacity, reliable message recovery, and strong semantic consistency under different channel conditions. In addition, eavesdroppers without the correct digital token cannot reliably recover the secret message, and the generated stego videos effectively resist the steganalysis detection. We further establish a prototype testbed to verify the practical feasibility of SemVideoSte.

title: LangNCO: Compiling Natural-Language Constraints into Inference-Time Interventions for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Hironori Ohigashi
abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered during training, but operational requirements may change after deployment and be communicated in natural language. We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-specific requirements into structured inference-time interventions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pretrained policy's architecture, learned input representation, or parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable semantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deterministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate violations but does not ensure that a complete feasible continuation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using controlled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% feasibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference gaps of 1.63--3.26%, 97.33--100% feasibility when separately generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and 98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These results demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, without retraining.

title: Towards High Semantic Fidelity: Hyperdimensional Symbolic Messages in Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Shoucheng Song; Chang Yao; Hao Wu; Youfang Lin; Sheng Han; Kai Lv
abstract: Semantic fidelity is essential for multi-agent communication under non-ideal channels, comprising transmission fidelity and conversion fidelity. Yet existing numerical and neural message formats cannot simultaneously achieve both. To address this, we propose a novel message format-\textbf{H}yperdimensional \textbf{S}ymbolic \textbf{M}essages (HSM) and its corresponding communication framework \textbf{Herm}. For transmission fidelity, Herm suppresses semantic entanglement via an entity-attribute-value structured encoding pipeline. For conversion fidelity, Herm first leverages a receiver-centric ego-binding mechanism to align semantics. Then, a similarity-aware dual-branch fusion module is proposed to prevent critical semantic dilution. To realize explicit message-semantic conversion, we devise an iterative decoding scheme via algebraic inverse operations. Experiments exhibit that Herm outperforms baselines across various noisy scenarios while maintaining superior structural readability.

title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
authors: Yedidel Louck
abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

title: Artificial Intelligence Framework for Drug-Target Affinity Prediction Using Deep Neural Networks and Integrated Molecular and Protein Feature Engineering
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Objective: To develop an artificial intelligence framework that integrates deep neural networks with molecular and protein feature engineering to accurately predict drug-target affinity, thereby supporting efficient computational drug discovery and therapeutic candidate identification.The proposed study employed a publicly available drug-target affinity dataset consisting of molecular SMILES representations, protein amino acid sequences, and experimentally determined affinity values, partitioned into training, validation, and testing subsets for model development.Material and Methods: A publicly available drug-target affinity dataset containing training, validation, and testing subsets was employed, in which molecular SMILES representations and protein sequences were converted into integrated numerical descriptors through feature engineering and standardized before model training.Subsequently, a Deep Neural Network (DNN) was developed to capture the complex relationships between the engineered molecular and protein features for accurate drug-target affinity prediction.Extracting representative features from molecular SMILES representations and protein sequences remains a major challenge in accurately predicting drug-target affinity.Capturing the complex nonlinear relationships between drug molecules and target proteins is further complicated by the high dimensionality and intricate nature of biological data.Results: To mitigate these challenges, a Deep Neural Network integrated with molecular and protein feature engineering was employed to effectively model complex drug-target interactions and enhance the accuracy of drug-target affinity prediction.The proposed Deep Neural Network efficiently learns complex nonlinear patterns from integrated molecular and protein features, thereby enhancing the accuracy of drug-target affinity prediction.The proposed Deep Neural Network achieved consistent performance across the training, validation, and testing datasets, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.6586, 0.6465, and 0.6343, respectively.The obtained R² scores of 0.2585, 0.2163, and 0.1599 demonstrate the model's capability to effectively predict drug-target affinity using integrated molecular and protein features.Conclusion: The proposed Artificial Intelligence framework effectively combined Deep Neural Networks with integrated molecular and protein feature engineering for drugtarget affinity prediction.The findings indicate that the framework provides a reliable and efficient approach for modelling drug-target interactions, thereby supporting computational drug discovery.

title: RegCL: Compact Continual SAM Adaptation for Visual Grounding in Multi-Sensorial Media
authors: Yuan-Chen Shu; Zi Lin; Xiaoyu Zhou; Yongtao Wang
abstract: Multi-sensorial media systems, including AR/VR, remote operation, and embodied AI, require visual grounding modules that remain reliable as sensing environments and application domains evolve. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) provides a strong foundation for dense visual segmentation, but its performance degrades on specialized and dynamically arriving domains such as medical imagery, camouflaged scenes, and shadow-dominant environments. Existing continual learning methods often rely on replay data or growing domain-specific modules, limiting compact deployment in evolving media pipelines. To address this issue, we propose RegCL, a non-replay continual adaptation framework that consolidates multi-domain segmentation knowledge into a single SAM adapter through incremental model merging. RegCL merges lightweight adaptation modules, e.g., LoRA-style AugModules, by optimizing prediction consistency between the merged model and domain-specific adapters while carrying forward compact historical feature statistics. Experiments across five heterogeneous segmentation datasets show that RegCL achieves strong retention and adaptation under domain-incremental learning, outperforming competitive non-replay continual learning and merging baselines. These results suggest that RegCL can serve as a compact visual adaptation component for evolving multi-sensorial media pipelines. The code is available at https://github.com/Anderw-S/RegCL

title: Systematic Mapping Study: Formal Verification of Hypervisors
authors: Lucas Ransan; Nikolaï Kosmatov; Frédéric Loulergue
abstract: Abstract Hypervisors are a fundamental building block of modern computing, supporting cloud infrastructures, virtualization platforms, and security-critical systems. They enable multiple operating systems to run on shared hardware while enforcing strong isolation. At the same time, their low-level position in the software stack makes them particularly sensitive: a single flaw can expose all hosted virtual machines and impact confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Establishing their correctness is therefore essential. In this context, formal verification provides a rigorous means to prove correctness and security properties, relying on mathematically sound foundations. This state-of-knowledge paper surveys existing work on the formal verification of hypervisors. It examines representative projects and approaches, comparing their verification scope, tools, and guarantees. The paper further identifies key challenges, including concurrency, low-level implementation details, and hardware interactions, and highlights current trends and future directions.

title: Chemogenetic inhibition of the ventrolateral orbitofrontal cortex disrupts novelty-guided updating of spatial memories and alters hippocampal engram reactivation
authors: K I Kim; Dawnbe Yu; William F Wade; Rowan Zdziarski-West; Z. Ahmad; Mikayla Cutler; Grace Romanelli; Adam Daki; Stephanie L. Grella
abstract: Abstract Rationale Adaptive behavior requires revising memories when outcomes deviate from expectations. The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is implicated in representing outcome expectancies, but its role in memory-updating, beyond value-based learning, remains unclear. Objectives We tested whether the ventrolateral OFC (VLO) contributes to hippocampal-dependent memory-updating in the Objects in Updated Locations (OUL) task, where novelty-driven exploration provides a behavioral readout consistent with successful updating of spatial information Methods Using inhibitory DREADDs, in male and female (Swiss Webster and C57BL/6) mice, we suppressed VLO activity during the Updating session, when new object-location information was introduced. Results Control mice preferentially explored the updated object-location configuration during Updating and discriminated between updated and novel object-location configurations at Test, whereas VLO-inhibited mice did not. VLO inhibition when no updating demand was present did not alter exploration of novel object-location configurations or memory for the original spatial configuration at Test. Conclusions These results indicate that VLO activity is selectively required when novelty must be interpreted relative to prior experience, implicating this region in evaluating change rather than detecting it. To assess hippocampal ensemble dynamics, we tagged neuronal ensembles, in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) recruited during Updating, followed by quantification of overlap between Updating-tagged cells and ensembles reactivated at Test. We found that VLO inhibition reduced reactivation of Updating-tagged dDG ensembles, paralleling the behavioral impairments observed in the OUL task. These findings support a role for the VLO in hippocampal-dependent memory-updating and extend OFC models beyond reward contexts to include predictive updating of spatial memory representations. Significance Statement Using a spatial paradigm that distinguishes detection of changed information from incorporation of that information into an updated hippocampal representation, we found that ventrolateral orbitofrontal cortex (VLO) activity is required for memory-updating when new information is present. We found behavioral deficits accompanied by impairments in hippocampal ensemble representations, indicating VLO activity is necessary for memory-updating at the hippocampal engram level. Through this mechanism, the OFC supports the flexible updating of expected outcomes when environmental conditions shift, allowing for the re-evaluation of previously learned associations. These findings extend models of orbitofrontal cortex function beyond reward-guided behavior and identify a cortical contribution to predictive spatial memory processes. Disruption of this computation may contribute to the cognitive rigidity observed in neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: From Emotion to Expression: The AL–DL–CL Framework for Understanding Communication in the Age of AI and Digital Media
authors: Chacko P. George
venue: International journal of civilizations studies & tolerance sciences.
abstract: Rapid progress in digital media and artificial intelligence is transforming human communication, facilitating the rapid exchange of messages and minimizing the chances of reflective interpretation. Existing theories in linguistics, psychology, and cultural studies address the structural, cognitive, or social aspects of language, yet fail to explain how emotional processing, internal linguistic structuring, and culturally mediated communication function as a coherent, dynamic system. Through this model, the authors present the AL–DL–CL framework that explores how three layers are engaged in a process that results in communication, through a recursive interaction between the Automatic Layer (AL), the Deliberate Layer (DL), and the Cultural Language Layer (CL). In such a process, the affective or unconscious processes in AL are consistently reframed into structured internal representations via DL, and through CL, and translated back into culturally-expressed language serves as a feedback mechanism, with a tendency to modify cognition and emotional response. Based on a multi-method exploratory approach of sequential cultural transmission, clinical case study analysis, and group-based validation, the results indicate that language is not so much a static container for meaning as a process of reconstruction that is molded by the dynamic interaction between emotion, cognition, and culture. This model also demonstrates how digitally mediated communication can amplify AL-directed reaction and limit DL-level thinking, which increases the potential for misinterpretation, polarization, or misinformation. The AL–DL–CL framework provides guidance in a unified theoretical perspective around language emergence, responsible AI design and digital literacy and intercultural discourse based on the continuous transformation system of communication, and not on the linear encoding.

title: Historical dynamics of social adaptation strategies under natural hazard characteristics in the Hengduan Mountains, Southwest China
authors: Xueyuan Huang; Yiping Fang; Xinjun He; Liang Emlyn Yang
abstract: The nexus between natural hazard events and regional societal responses constitutes a critical link in the chain of climate change impacts on human social systems. China’s extensive historical documentary resources remain underutilized for reconstructing spatiotemporal patterns of natural hazard events, characterizing impacts, and identifying adaptation features. This study systematically compiles a dataset of natural hazard events in the Hengduan Mountains region (HMR) during the Little Ice Age (LIA), and delineates their spatiotemporal patterns across climatic fluctuations. An examination of societal adaptation across ten stages reveals the transformation of traditional mountain societies from infrastructure restoration to integrated hazard-relief systems. Results indicate that natural hazard events in the HMR exhibit phased clustering, with one primary peak and four secondary peaks. These clusters are concentrated in land-water ecotones, forming three coupled hazard zones: tectonic-dominated, agroecologically vulnerable, and monsoon-sensitive hydrological zones. Temporal analyses demonstrate the dominance of hydro-meteorological hazard events and their strong association with climate. Seismic geological hazard events show strong spatial congruence with active fault zones. In contrast, hot-spots of biological hazard events exhibit strong spatial coupling with food-security events. The Driving forces-Pressures-State-Impacts-Responses (DPSIR) framework reveals that the combined effects of climate transitions and mountain development exert environmental pressures on regional systems, thereby contributing to cascading hazard-chain effects and livelihood disruption. In traditional societies, dynamic adaptation strategies evolved through sophisticated spatiotemporally tailored measures, localized knowledge transmission, and the establishment of synergies between institutions and culture. This research advances understanding of social adaptation strategies to natural hazards, thereby providing historical references for environmental decision-making and hazard prevention.

title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Thi-Nhung Nguyen; Viet-Thanh Pham; Linhao Luo; Thuy-Trang Vu; Dinh Phung
abstract: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.

title: Memento: Communicating Sensor Observations Through Shared Memory
authors: Chae Young Lee; Lan Mei; Yifan Yang; Sara Achour; Zerina Kapetanovic
abstract: Wireless sensing systems often transmit highly redundant observations, making communication a bottleneck for low-power devices. We present Memento, a communication system that exploits recurring content by transmitting observations by reference. The sender embeds each observation and searches a shared vector table stored in persistent memory. When it finds a sufficiently similar prior observation, it sends a compact reference; otherwise, it sends the observation itself and adds it to the table. This design shifts work from wireless communication to local computation and storage, without requiring a fixed task-specific model. We implement Memento on a microcontroller with an SD card and evaluate it on three image datasets and one radar dataset. Memento provides favorable accuracy-communication and accuracy-energy tradeoffs against compression-based and task-oriented baselines. At high-accuracy operating points, it matches cloud classification accuracy on three workloads while using 5.5 to 27.1 times less energy, and comes within 0.14 percentage points on a fourth while using 14.7 times less energy. These results show that retrieval over persistent local memory can reduce communication costs in recurrent sensing workloads.

title: RetinaSC: Retinal Semantic Communication Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Detection
authors: Avani Shinod; Rangineni Rushitha; Asqeem Nas; Anirban Bhowal; Shikha Baghel
abstract: This paper presents a lightweight semantic com- munication framework for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading from fundus images pertaining specifically to the APTOS2019 dataset. The framework includes semantic encoder designed using ResNet34, U-Net, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-B0 architectures. Further, the trained models are used to train the same framework for IDRiD dataset using transfer learning approach. Such a framework will enable the telemedicine sector in the early detection of DR and prevent total blindness. The results reveal that for APTOS, task-oriented semantic systems can achieve satisfactory robust performance (more than 0.8 weighted F1 score for ResNet34 and EfficientNet-B0) across different channels. In particular, considering the trade-off between complexity, latency, throughput, and F1 score, MobileNetV2 is the best model with weighted F1 score of 0.76-0.78 for both task and reconstruction- oriented modules and end-to-end latency of only 8.162 ms.

title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
authors: Yuquan Xiao; Qinghe Du; Chaoyang Zhang; Wenchi Cheng; Jingqing Wang; Tao Chen; Jiangzhou Wang
abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.

title: RFWeave: Learning Wireless Propagation Across Scenes and Transceiver Configurations
authors: Shurui Xu; Xiao Ye; Yijie Bian; Junjie Ai; Yuxuan Chen; Weicong Chen; Wankai Tang; Shi Jin
abstract: Wireless propagation modeling is foundational to the evaluation and design of modern communication systems. To achieve accurate wireless propagation prediction, recent learning-based approaches leverage scene geometry and materials, demonstrating promising generalization across transceiver locations and unseen scenes. However, these approaches remain largely confined to a fixed configuration of array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. In this work, we introduce RFWeave, a learned wireless propagation model designed to generalize across scenes, transceiver locations, and transceiver configurations. To accommodate varying array structures, RFWeave incorporates variable-length transceiver tokens that represent antenna elements individually. Furthermore, to capture the geometry between transmit and receive antenna elements, RFWeave aggregates their pairwise spatial relations into propagation tokens. A configuration-conditioned decoder predicts the spatial spectrum and received power. RFWeave is trained on a large-scale simulated dataset spanning 10,000 indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records under diverse transceiver configurations. Extensive evaluations show that RFWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated generalization settings, improving spatial spectrum structural similarity (SSIM) by up to 15.7% and reducing received power mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 35.4% over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes. Additional experiments on measured DICHASUS data and in beam management further demonstrate RFWeave's broader applicability to real-world channels and downstream wireless tasks.

title: More Interactions Make Communications More Efficient: A Directed Information Bottleneck Approach to Task-Oriented Communication
authors: Zhirun Zheng; Yiqin Deng; Phone Lin; Yuguang Fang
abstract: Task-oriented communication improves communication efficiency by transmitting semantic information required for downstream tasks, but may incur redundancy with previously transmitted information. To address this issue, we propose a variational directed information bottleneck joint source-channel coding (VDIB-JSCC) framework that transmits only previously unacquired information. Specifically, we use directed information to characterize the causal flow of task-relevant incremental information and theoretically demonstrate its advantages over mutual information and conditional mutual information. Based on this metric, we formulate a directed information bottleneck (DIB) objective that balances task-relevant information preservation and redundant information compression. We further derive a variational formulation, termed VDIB, whose tractable upper bound serves as the training loss. The encoder integrates a Vision Transformer for frame-wise semantic extraction and a Mamba-based causal state-space model for capturing temporal dependencies and extracting incremental information, while the decoder uses a Mamba-based state-space model for task inference. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 video streams demonstrate that VDIB-JSCC achieves higher classification accuracy with less transmitted information than state-of-the-art semantic communication methods. These results show that leveraging historical knowledge enables task completion with less information, improving communication efficiency.

title: CreepScope: Measuring Post-Use Authorization Exposure in Tool-Using Agents
authors: Haoran Yu; Lifei Liu; Danping Zhang; Su Wang; Pin Qian; Yihang Chen; Xiaochong Jiang
abstract: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. We study this lifecycle failure as privilege creep: a capability stays reachable after its last justified workflow step. We present CreepScope, a trace-oriented evaluation protocol that samples reachable authority at every step and separates no-remaining-use exposure into stale-after-use and never-required components; Capability-Step Exposure (CSE) counts total stepwise overexposure and Residual Privilege Debt (RPD) the terminal residue, while stale-after-use exposure is the direct privilege-creep measure. A 96-cell deterministic replay over 12 controlled storage, communication, and cloud-operation workflows validates these semantics: Static Task Scope and Monotonic On-Demand retain mean CSEs of 26 and 13, whereas an oracle-controlled Step Lease has zero CSE and zero residual debt by construction. All three persistent regimes share the same stale-after-use exposure of 13, so their CSE differences come from scope and grant timing rather than post-use retention; Full Access alone adds 91.33 never-required capability-steps. A separate 24-episode local case then lets Qwen2 7B choose tools in one simulated mail workflow: the injected stale send executes in all nine persistent-policy episodes and in none of the three Step-Lease episodes, while all 24 required action sequences complete. These results establish a reproducible containment case, not cross-workflow or cross-model effectiveness. Core metrics are reconstructed from raw events, and exact gates reject incomplete or duplicated evaluation grids.

title: Radio Echo Representation Learning for Semantic Sensing in Multi-Modal ISAC Systems
authors: Guanping Shang; Anzheng Tang; Kwok Kit Chan; Shenghui Song
abstract: Semantic sensing extends integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) beyond physical parameter estimation by exploiting task-oriented representations from radio echoes. Nevertheless, existing multimodal sensing remains largely limited to vision-assisted radio physical parameter estimation or typically processes the visual and radio modalities separately, leaving radio representations underutilized for visual task enhancement. Feature-level fusion enables closer cross-modal interaction, while echo interference complicates the learning of user-specific radio representations and its semantic consistency with the visual entities. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a multimodal semantic sensing framework for orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)-ISAC systems. We propose a radio encoder to learn radio representations oriented toward visual localization from superimposed pilot echoes, together with Variational Radio-Visual Grounding (VRVG) to promote semantic consistency between the learned radio representations and visual spatial features. The radio representations are then formulated as semantic probes to highlight the corresponding entities in the visual scene through cross-modal fusion. Experiments using real-world RCooper dataset show that the resulting synergistic radio-visual embeddings enable accurate radio-visual user matching and significantly improve both user-specific visual localization and physical parameter estimation performance. The results substantiate the benefits of radio representation learning and semantically consistent fusion for multimodal semantic sensing.

title: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Korean Language Learning: Applications, Challenges, and Instructional Strategies
authors: Yundong Wu
abstract: This conceptual narrative review examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Korean language learning. The paper synthesizes recent scholarship on AI-assisted language learning, Korean language education, technology acceptance, and educational ethics to develop an analytical framework for responsible classroom use. The review focuses on four dimensions: Korean language skills, Korean-specific linguistic and cultural features, instructional design, and governance risks. The analysis suggests that generative AI can support listening, speaking, reading, and writing when tasks are explicitly designed around Korean phonology, morphology, pragmatics, and learner purposes such as TOPIK preparation, study abroad, employment, and popular-culture engagement. It also identifies challenges in cultural-pragmatic accuracy, hallucinated expressions, assessment validity, data privacy, unequal access, teacher readiness, and learner dependency. The paper concludes that generative AI should function as a mediated learning resource rather than a substitute for teachers, learner judgment, or culturally grounded interaction.

title: Research on Attention Guidance and User Autonomy in AI-Powered Immersive Environments
authors: Mulin Qiao
abstract: As artificial intelligence gets deeply embedded into immersive environments, attention-guiding technology delivers ever more precise and efficient outcomes. Still, this improved efficiency carries an overlooked design risk: excessive AI guidance may steadily erode user agency and undermine exploratory behaviors as well as the process of meaning-making. This paper builds a critical conceptual framework to rethink attention-oriented design within AI-driven immersive settings. It defines excessive guidance and establishes theoretical links between this concept and three core facets of user agency: perceived control, voluntary choice and decision-making authority. Based on these findings, the paper calls for a paradigm shift from attention optimization to curiosity-led design. It also puts forward actionable behavioral measurement indicators covering exploration scope, average dwell time, path-following ratio, active choice frequency and recall test performance. The proposed framework supplies a new theoretical tool for human-computer interaction research in immersive scenarios and helps shift AI's role from a fixed route provider to an exploratory collaborator.

title: Antitrust Regulation of Algorithmic "Platform-Driven Involution'': From Governing the Corporate Person to Governing the Platform Ecosystem
authors: Sida Zeng
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly govern competition through algorithmically administered rules that allocate visibility, subsidies, commissions, participation opportunities, and sanctions. This article reconstructs ``platform-driven involution'' as a testable, portfolio-based theory-of-harm framework rather than a freestanding antitrust offense. Its application remains anchored in market definition, dominance, identified conduct under Article 22 of China's Anti-Monopoly Law, causal proof, competitive effects, and objective justification. The article clarifies that ecosystem analysis supplements rather than replaces relevant-market analysis and develops an evidence architecture for separating platform-induced effects from macroeconomic, demand, cost, and merchant-specific confounders. It then distinguishes preventive measures already supported by Chinese hard law or voluntary compliance guidance from compulsory competition-specific filing and pre-deployment assessment that would require clearer future authorization. The 2026 Trip.com decision is used to show how traffic allocation, exclusivity, lowest-price requirements, technical monitoring, and sanctions can form an integrated abuse architecture while liability remains tied to established statutory categories. Comparative analysis of EU platform regulation and Google Shopping supports calibrated procedural prevention, meaningful explanation, and causal discipline without protecting inefficient competitors or condemning aggressive competition.

title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
authors: Hongyu Xia
abstract: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-performance validation.

title: TinZr: A compact wireless ESP32-C3 platform for multi-modal physiological sensor integration and data acquisition.

title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Sajjad Baghaee; Aimin Li; Shanmugarajan Balasubramanian; Elif Uysal
abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $Δ_i^e(t)=[Δ_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $Δ_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.

title: Goal-Oriented Ordered Autoencoding for Successive Refinement in Progressive Communication
authors: Qi Liao; Dario Bega
abstract: Goal-oriented communication often struggles to sustain downstream task performance under variable and unpredictable bandwidth. We address this problem by proposing GO-OAE (Goal-Oriented Ordered AutoEncoding), which learns a progressively refinable quantized latent sequence, optimized directly for task utility rather than source reconstruction. Each component of the sequence is represented for transmission by its code index, and the learned ordering enables inference from any received prefix of the index sequence, with performance improving as more indices arrive. We prove that optimizing the goal-oriented distortion objective is equivalent to solving a weighted conditional information bottleneck formulation, and introduce an unbiased multi-prefix importance sampling (MPIS) estimator, to reduce GO-OAE training computational cost from O(BK) to O(Bm) with m << K, and reduces the estimator variance by a factor of 1/m. Experiments show that, on MiniImageNet, GO-OAE achieves over 96% of the lossless upper-bound classification accuracy using 324 bits per image (683X compression vs. raw RGB), and already attains over 94% of the upper bound with only 70% of the transmitted indices. It consistently outperforms reconstruction-optimized codecs and ordered autoencoders trained with uniform prefix sampling across all transmission budgets, demonstrating effective communication at extreme compression rates.

title: Behavior-Mining, Generative Conversations, and Collaborative Advisory: the Future of Travel and Tourism Recommender Systems
authors: Alejandro Bellogín; Linus W. Dietz; Francesco Ricci; Pablo Sánchez
abstract: Since the early adoption of e-commerce, travel and tourism has been a lab for the design of recommender systems: tools that help travelers choose destinations, flights, accommodations, and combine them into itineraries. Data-driven recommendation techniques, ranging from case-based reasoning to reinforcement learning, have been adapted to travelers' needs. The research community has produced multifaceted prototypes of travel and tourism recommender systems (TTRSs), which are context-dependent, multistakeholder-oriented, and more recently, addressing sustainability issues, such as overtourism. Despite this enduring work, TTRSs are not widespread yet. We argue that three limitations can explain this: outdated and sparse data sets used to train and validate TTRSs, algorithms that prioritize prediction accuracy over domain-specific dimensions such as novelty and contextual relevance, and a failure to address the specific needs of travelers. Targeted incremental research could address these limitations, but a disruptive factor has meanwhile entered the ecosystem of tourism information and commercialization platforms: generative artificial intelligence. According to market research, GenAI applications are becoming the primary entry point for travelers planning their trips. This forces research to rethink how TTRSs should be designed and which core techniques should be integrated. We claim that future TTRSs, in addition to offering personalized information filtering, should become more flexible advisors that support decision making, integrating multiple data types and AI techniques, from data mining to natural language processing. Moreover, they must transparently balance the conflicting goals of travelers, service suppliers, platform owners, and local communities. We then outline research targets for building more effective TTRSs, fruitfully combining old and new recommendation techniques.

title: Mission Efficiency Optimization in Low-Altitude Economy: Adaptive Power Allocation for Coordinating Heterogeneous Aircraft Swarms
authors: Jiarui Zhang; Wei Feng; Chao Dong; Ning Ge; Qihui Wu
abstract: With the rapid development of the low-altitude economy, low-altitude operations are booming, where complex missions require collaborative efforts among multiple heterogeneous low-altitude aircrafts (LAAs). Specifically, different LAAs assume distinct roles: some for sensing, some for communication, some for computing, and others for mission execution, together forming a sensing-communication-computing-control (SC3) closed loop, akin to a reflex arc. To enable efficient coordination in such multi-LAA swarms, we introduce the concept of operational-capability entropy (OCE) to quantify the effective work capability of operational LAAs. Accordingly, by jointly considering heterogeneous OCE and channel conditions among LAAs, we formulate the power allocation problem with the goal of minimizing the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost, which serves as a metric for mission efficiency. The resulting complex optimization problem is decomposed into two convex subproblems that are solved iteratively, with closed-form solutions derived for each. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed mission-oriented adaptive power allocation scheme significantly outperforms traditional ones.

title: Resource-Efficient Semantic Communication for Heterogeneous Agentic Teams
authors: Farhad Rezazadeh; Hatim Chergui; Lingjia Liu; Merouane Debbah; Merouane Abdelkader Debbah
abstract: Teams of autonomous agents, including large language model (LLM) agents, must coordinate over scarce and unreliable wireless links. We propose goal-oriented semantic communication (GOSC), a closed-loop co-design that jointly decides what each agent sends, when it sends it, and how reliably it is transmitted, based on each message's value to the team task. An edge broadcast of the team's common knowledge closes the loop by updating these values. We prove that a message is sent only if its value exceeds the cost of delivering it and that more valuable messages receive more robust transmission rates, and we show that the scheduler solves each scheduling step exactly whenever the radio budget is not saturated, which held in 95% of scheduling decisions. In search-and-rescue missions validated on unseen scenarios, GOSC meets the same mission targets as carefully tuned periodic semantic schemes with 1.2--8.5 times fewer uplink channel uses. In most settings, this advantage persists with realistic packet overheads, reaching 16.6 times fewer uplink channel uses and 13.8 times lower cost when downlink costs are included; in the rescue task, it also persists when all agents share one uplink. Rough value estimates suffice, whereas values that ignore message content can fail. With three different LLMs, GOSC uses 3.2--3.5 times fewer channel uses, while completion-time gains depend on the model.
