title: A2SSC: An Agent-based Adaptive Semantic Speech Communication System
authors: Dongxu Yang; Fangyu Liu; Peiwen Jiang; Li Xiao; Shi Jin
abstract: Abstract In wireless environments with weak coverage or rapidly changing channels, reliable speech transmission is challenging due to fluctuating channel quality and limited bandwidth. Semantic communication offers a promising solution by focusing on the transmission of essential information rather than raw signals. Although existing semantic speech communication systems have made progress, they still lack decision mechanisms that are aware of both content and channel, limiting their robustness and flexibility. In this paper, we propose an agent-based adaptive semantic speech communication system (A2SSC). The system encodes textual content and speaker characteristics separately, and adaptively allocates transmission resources based on the importance of the speech content and the current channel conditions. At the same time, we incorporate an agent-based architecture to ensure system flexibility and scalability, and introduce an online learning mechanism that allows the system to continuously adapt to changing channel conditions after deployment. Experimental results show that A2SSC achieves comparable word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SS) to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing the maximum num-ber of transmitted symbols by 62.5%. Moreover, the system maintains robust performance across varying channel conditions, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable and efficient speech transmission in challenging wireless environments.

title: Machine-Learned Mismatch and Task Preservation Beliefs in CoSMA DAI for Common Knowledge Aware Semantic Alignment
authors: Iacovos I. Ioannou; Chrıstophoros Christophorou; Marios Raspopoulos; Vasos Vassiliou
abstract: Correct packet delivery does not guarantee correct semantic interpretation when endpoint meanings for the same learned codeword diverge. CoSMA DAI is proposed for mismatch detection, protected confirmation, task preservation and semantic repair. Channel-conditioned global evidence, semantic class local evidence, temporal dynamics, channel context and protected probe evidence are fused by a causal machine-learned mismatch belief. A transmitter-derived task belief preserves the downstream decision while repair is pending and BDIx agents select guarded intentions for probing, fallback and resynchronisation. Evaluation uses 30 held-out drift seeds, 300 matched null streams and 300 degrading channel controls. Six referenced sequential monitors receive the same conditioned payload score. CoSMA DAI obtains 100.00 percent balanced accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and Matthews correlation coefficient with zero observed matched null false alarms. Its aggregate delay is 5.62 slots, compared with 11.58 slots for the other zero false alarm method. The task-preservation belief maintains 94.73 percent task accuracy through every divergence scenario, above the quantised accuracy ceiling of 0.919 of the semantic path, because it is derived from the unquantised transmitter latent. A task-label-only control confirms that this accuracy is secured by the preservation belief alone, independently of the detector, so task preservation and mismatch detection are decoupled by design and detectors are compared on residual functional semantic outage, outage duration and semantic reconstruction fidelity, which measure the restoration of the semantic representation itself. Without repair, the residual semantic outage is 73.69 percent at 15.97 dB reconstruction fidelity, whereas CoSMA DAI reduces it to 0.73 percent over 6.62 slots at 21.74 dB. Under five declared parity tiers, in which multivariate and supervised baselines receive the identical features, training seeds, protected probe and candidate budget, the protected confirmation stage reduces false repair for every detector to which it is attached. Zero-shot evaluation over 7 unseen mismatch families and 5 unseen link models retains full detection with zero observed false repair in 6 of the 7 families and on every link and identifies receiver-side decoder drift as a condition the present observation model cannot detect. The learned belief is validated at slot level with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.99997 and a class overlap of 0.00039, leave-one-mechanism-out and cross-channel retraining are reported, behaviour is characterised down to the practical detection boundary and scaling to 64-dimensional representations with 2048-entry codebooks is demonstrated. The task-belief mechanism is shown to be economical only for small closed-set output spaces and the channel-conditioning tables are shown to reduce to 6 cells without loss. Every comparator is additionally retuned on the same development budget, paired bootstrap intervals and signed-rank tests are reported over the shared streams, auxiliary traffic and radio energy are normalised per correct decision, authentication of the task belief is specified and charged and transfer to MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 is demonstrated without retraining, including on a convolutional VQ-VAE representation with a jointly learned 512-entry codebook, where foreground segmentation and localisation are restored to within the quantisation limit while a class decision cannot serve either task. The control traffic share is 23.59 percent, which is 12.62 percent lower than the monitor value. The additional semantic side information increases radio energy to 0.393 mJ per stream and reduces control-adjusted resource efficiency to 6.203 source-equivalent bits per channel use. The results therefore establish reliable detection and semantic repair within the principal comparison, with comparator-specific delay advantages and without claiming task-accuracy, semantic-rate or energy superiority.

title: Channel-adaptive semantic token transmission for multimodal edge perception over wireless uplinks
authors: Yong Liao; Zhiyuan Zhu; Dapeng Wu; Ruyan Wang

title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Karol Budzyn; Adrian Brodzik; Mateusz Szczepkowski
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

title: LLM-Guided Dual-Stage Latency Optimization for Closed-Loop 6G V2I Digital Twins
authors: Liu Cao; Peide Li; Yuan Yang; Zhaoyu Liu; Lyutianyang Zhang; Jinke Ren; Shuguang Cui
abstract: Wireless Digital Twins are emerging as a key enabler for predictive network control in 6G Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) systems. However, closed-loop V2I DTs face two dual-stage communication bottlenecks arising from model parameter exchange for V2I DT reconstruction and multi-service V2I traffic delivery after each reconstruction. This paper proposes a closed-loop dual-stage End-to-End (E2E) latency optimization framework that integrates Compressed Personalized Federated Learning with a unified Large-Language-Model-guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning approach. A CPFL-enabled decision-oriented V2I DT is first constructed by jointly predicting Path Loss (PL) and Quality-of-Experience (QoE)-oriented Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Then the framework comprises two temporally coupled but latency-wise distinct optimization stages: Stage I minimizes the joint Uplink (UL) and Downlink (DL) E2E transmission latency of compressed shared backbone's parameters, and Stage II minimizes the service-aware E2E latency of multi-service V2I traffic. As the two stages share aligned agent roles and action space, we develop a unified Semantic-Aware Guidance-Enhanced Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization framework, in which the LLM acts as a training-time semantic planner that provides high-level traffic splitting and power allocation guidance to reduce inefficient exploration, while the MARL agents execute feasible low-level actions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables efficient V2I DT reconstruction and significantly reduces both E2E latency for DT reconstruction and multi-service V2I traffic. The proposed SAGE-MAPPO supports cross-stage policy reuse by sequentially solving the two stages within each DT update cycle, which accelerates convergence relative to the existing baselines and facilitates timely DT updates in dynamic V2I scenarios.
arxiv_comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. 15 pages, 8 figures

title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
authors: Sergio Burdisso; Esaú Villatoro-Tello; Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés; Yanis Labrak; Jordi Luque; Milos Cernak; Petr Motlicek
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

title: Mobility-Budget-Constrained Submodular Maximization for Distributed Semantic Multi-Robot Exploration
authors: Changxuan Yao; Sandilya Sai Garimella; Lu Gan; Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: Multi-robot exploration under communication and mobility constraints requires balancing information gain with reachability. We present a distributed semantic exploration framework that combines Dirichlet mapping, budget-constrained trajectory selection, and Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) coordination. Each robot clusters frontiers, computes terrain- and heading-aware least-cost paths with a single budget-limited Dijkstra search, and selects feasible paths by marginal information gain, represented by the expected reduction in Dirichlet entropy. Each robot's per-round selection is exact, the team's joint per-round information gain is at least half the centralized optimum, and the bound degrades gracefully under limited communication. Ten-run gridworld ablations show improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty with lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance frontier selection. Budget-sensitivity experiments show that an intermediate budget best balances path reach and receding-horizon execution. In photorealistic full-system simulation against five coordination rules run in their native published forms, the proposed method attains the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy while being the only one that respects the per-trajectory mobility budget.
arxiv_comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to the IROS 2026 SeMaNa Workshop. The first two authors contributed equally

title: LURE: a Phase-Labelled Synthetic Corpus of Online-Grooming Exchanges
authors: Emanuele Florindi; Valentina Franzoni; Ludovico Guercio; Alfredo Milani; Mattia Polticchia
abstract: Phase-annotated conversational data is essential for studying the progression of online grooming of minors and for developing early warning tools. However, the only publicly available source (i.e., Perverted-Justice archive, which contains a subset coded using ChatCoder) is small, outdated, and frozen. We present a synthetic corpus of groomer-victim exchanges, generated using a retrieval-augmented pipeline running on institutional hardware. This pipeline uses an openly available, eight-billion-parameter, refusal-ablated language model. The corpus was created using the five stages of the responsible-generation protocol for synthetic datasets: ontology-driven design based on the ChatCoder luring-communication scheme (eight communicative tags mapped onto four grooming phases); multi-model prompt testing; human-in-the-loop supervision; semantic and feature-level validation; and modality-aware documentation. The released corpus contains 2,121 unique exchanges across seven tags and four phases, each accompanied by a Plutchik emotion field. Validation quantifies the integrity and lexical profile of the corpus, as well as the reproduction of real seed lines, in-domain label recoverability (tag accuracy: 0.85; phase accuracy: 0.93) and its transfer to real ChatCoder offender lines, which were coded automatically at the eight-tag level (31,640 lines) and by human coders at the three-construct level (10,876 posts). Accuracy was measured for lexical and sentence-embedding features, while a real-versus-synthetic discriminator was able to separate the two domains with 91% accuracy. The scope of the corpus includes controlled, phase-conditioned experimentation, pipeline development and augmentation alongside real data and awareness material. The corpus, its datasheet and the audit code are released with vetted access.

title: Adaptive Role Assignment and Controlled Feature Reconstruction for Federated Image Semantic Communication
authors: Yuxuan Chen; Jiao Bie; Hang Qi; Jingjin Wu
abstract: Hybrid federated semantic communication enables user equipment (UEs) to contribute model updates or semantic features under a shared training framework. However, heterogeneous role costs and the interaction between model aggregation and feature reconstruction (FR) remain key challenges in practical radio access network (RAN) deployment. To address these issues, we propose ARC-FedSC, a RAN-aware framework that coordinates UE role assignment and server-side controlled FR under a fixed communication budget. Within ARC-FedSC, RAN Aware Role-Bandit learns the historical contribution of UEs in different roles together with current uplink conditions, while Temporal Consistency Alignment (TCA) regulates FR according to recent model aggregation directions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with time-varying RAN channels show that ARC-FedSC outperforms baselines across all five tested role configurations in the later training stage, with the best configurations achieving about 24.17 dB average PSNR over the last 20 rounds. Component level results further show that Role-Bandit maintains an average rolling UE coverage of 85.3%, compared with about 65.7% for baseline, while TCA reduces the probability of harmful FR events from 0.245 to 0.093, corresponding to a 62.0% reduction. Ablation and sensitivity studies further support the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed design.

title: Tutorial on Closed-Loop and Application-Aware Digital Twins for Future Wireless Networks
authors: Yuchen Liu; Sara Garcia Sanchez; Mingzhe Chen; Xingqin Lin; Berk Canberk; Tommaso Melodia
abstract: To support emerging applications such as extended reality, autonomous systems, and large-scale cyber-physical infrastructures, next-generation wireless networks must evolve beyond traditional communication paradigms toward tightly integrated and closed-loop systems. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have recently emerged as a key enabler of this transformation by bridging the physical and digital worlds through real-time, bidirectional interactions and adaptive control mechanisms. In this tutorial, we provide a comprehensive overview of DTN design and optimization across multiple system dimensions. Specifically, we first introduce the fundamental design principles of DTN creation, including high-fidelity twin modeling, telemetry integration, and cyber-physical synchronization. We then present resource optimization and semantic-driven DTNs, where application-aware objectives and semantic abstractions guide efficient data processing, communication, and decision-making. Subsequently, we explore physical-layer optimization techniques for DTNs, emphasizing joint sensing, communication, and adaptive wireless resource control. Furthermore, we examine DTN-guided network management and feedback optimization, focusing on closed-loop learning, real-time control, and reinforcement-driven adaptation between digital twins and physical networks. Finally, we review ongoing standardization efforts and enabling tools that support the practical deployment of DTNs in real-world systems. This tutorial aims to provide a unified perspective on DTNs as an emerging paradigm for application-aware, AI-native, and closed-loop wireless systems, and to highlight key challenges and future research directions in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Accelerating MoE Training through Expert Placement and Replica Coordination
authors: Zhiqiang Tan; Maoxin Wang; Wenxiang Lin; Sijie Wang; Qiang Wang; Shaohuai Shi; Bo Li
abstract: Distributed training of sparsely activated mixture-of-experts (MoE) models is often bottlenecked by workload imbalance and all-to-all (A2A) communication induced by dynamic token routing. Existing token deduplication, expert placement, and replication techniques alleviate these bottlenecks but do not jointly capture their distinct load semantics. Under hierarchical token deduplication, communication counts each token once per destination group at each hierarchy level, whereas expert computation processes every token-expert assignment. With replication, both costs depend jointly on physical layout and token-to-copy mapping, making separate optimization suboptimal. We present PlaceMoE to address this coupling. First, we formulate the joint optimization of expert layout and source-aware token-to-copy mapping for E experts distributed across P devices, accounting for both hierarchical communication traffic and expert-compute load. Second, we develop a solver that combines co-selection-aware expert grouping, bounded dynamic programming for replica allocation, and alternating refinement of layout and mapping. Third, PlaceMoE overlaps replica-gradient synchronization with attention backward. We evaluate PlaceMoE on a 32-GPU cluster and a 64-NPU cluster using Qwen3-VL and DeepSeek-V3. Experimental results show that PlaceMoE achieves up to a 6.94x speedup in A2A communication and 1.74-2.33x speedups in end-to-end training over the state-of-the-art training framework VeOmni.

title: Protecting Shared Agent Workflows from Invalidation Attacks with Signed Trajectories and Runtime Verification
authors: Ruixiao Li; Fahao Chen; Peng Li
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on shared workflow repositories to transfer experience across tasks and agents. By abstracting past executions into reusable workflow graphs, such systems significantly improve planning efficiency and generalization. However, this emerging paradigm introduces a new and underexplored security risk: if the shared repository is compromised, tampered workflows can systematically mislead downstream agents, inducing persistent execution failures or unsafe behaviors. In this work, we present a principled protection framework for shared agent workflows based on signed trajectories and runtime verification. We require all cloud-collected trajectories used for workflow generation to be cryptographically signed, with each trajectory representing a concrete execution instance. Prior to repository inclusion, trajectories undergo a unified screening process to ensure correctness and validity. When an agent retrieves a workflow from the shared repository, it also obtains a small set of signed supporting trajectories and verifies both their cryptographic integrity and their semantic consistency with the workflow. To make this practical for branching workflows, we further propose a runtime, path-aware retrieval strategy that dynamically fetches only the signed trajectories relevant to the execution path actually taken by the agent, substantially reducing communication and verification overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates, degrading agent inference performance by up to 73.16 percentage points in accuracy without effective workflow protection. In addition, the proposed protection achieves an average F1 score of 85.26% and a detection rate of 79.97%, outperforming existing baselines by about 2.02x.

title: Identifying and Prioritizing the Components of Circular Accounting: A Qualitative Study Based on Systematic Content Analysis
authors: Iran Fakhrinezhad; nemat rastgoo; Nemat Rostami Mazouei; Artin Beytari
abstract: The expansion of the circular economy has increased the need to transform accounting systems and identify the components required to support decision-making and reporting related to efficient resource utilization, waste reduction, and environmental performance. Despite the growing body of research on circular accounting, its constituent components and dimensions have been addressed in a fragmented manner across different studies, highlighting the need to identify and integrate these components. The present study aimed to identify, categorize, and prioritize the components of circular accounting. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of methodology, it employed a qualitative, descriptive–analytical approach. To collect the data, scientific publications and texts related to circular accounting, the circular economy, sustainability, environmental accounting, and material flow management were systematically reviewed. During the analytical stage, conventional qualitative content analysis was used to extract relevant concepts from the texts, code them, and organize them into categories and subcomponents based on conceptual similarity. Through the process of analyzing and integrating the codes, three main categories were identified: dynamic capabilities of circular accounting, material flows in the circular economy, and institutional–environmental drivers and barriers. Subsequently, 12 subcomponents were extracted and classified: flexibility and reconfiguration; innovation and technology; learning and knowledge development; interaction and accountability; efficient material management and consumption; life cycle and environmental traceability; supply chain and resource optimization; policymakers and regulations; infrastructure and information technology; culture, education, and media; economic incentives and market pressure; and organizational and coordination barriers. To prioritize the main categories, the frequency of the extracted codes was used as the prioritization criterion. The results showed that institutional–environmental drivers and barriers, with 29 codes accounting for 45.2% of the total, had the highest frequency, followed by the dynamic capabilities of circular accounting, with 22 codes and a 34.3% share, and material flows in the circular economy, with 13 codes and a 20.3% share. The findings indicate that the formation and development of circular accounting depend not only on internal accounting capabilities but also on institutional and environmental factors, technological infrastructure, policies and regulations, culture, and coordination among stakeholders. The findings of this study can provide a basis for developing a conceptual framework and designing measurement instruments for circular accounting in future studies.

title: THE AUTOMATED ADMINISTRATION MAGAZINE
authors: Ellinor Blom Lussi; Jonas Ledendal; Béatrice Schütte; Jockum Hildén; Terhi Esko; Sofia Heikkonen; Anne Kaun; Ida Koivisto; Suvi Sankari; Helmi Soininvaara; Katja de Vries; Kasia Söderlund; Riikka Koulu
abstract: This magazine disseminates project results from a four-year research project on governance of AI and automated decision-making in the public sector. The Automated Administration (ADM-GOV) is a project with researchers from Swedish and Finnish universities, led by Lund University and funded by the Future Challenges in the Nordics Programme.For the past four years, we have been studying how AI and automated decision-making (ADM) can be implemented in the public sector without undermining fundamental rights, good governance, and trust in public institutions. You find results from studies on various related aspects reported on in this magazine – in articles, commentaries and interviews. In addition, given the impact AI tools have on the very means for production of texts, images and graphic design, in what we think of as a formative period, a secondary purpose with this magazine has been to conduct a meta exploration of normative boundaries of how AI impacts human creative output. By pointing to normative boundaries, we argue that some of the changes in norms – legal but importantly also informally social – are somewhat blurry at the moment, and in need of clarifying explorations. Check it out!

title: Data Sherpa: An AI-Powered Assistant for Scientific Collaboration Knowledge Management
authors: Fabian Araneda Baltierra; F. Menanteau
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large scientific collaborations face a persistent challenge: critical knowledge is scattered across hundreds of people, documents, datasets, and communication archives, creating steep learning curves and inefficiencies that disproportionately affect early-career researchers and newcomers. Senior scientists are repeatedly drawn away from high-impact research to answer the same operational questions, while valuable institutional knowledge risks being lost as collaborations sunset. Data Sherpa is an open-source, AI-powered assistant designed to address these challenges by providing researchers with fast, accurate, and context-aware access to collaboration-specific knowledge. The current proof-of-concept demonstrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over Dark Energy Survey (DES) documentation, publications, and technical material, using vector embedding and semantic search with a PostgreSQL-based vector store (pgvector). Since submission, the project has shifted architecture: rather than continue building orchestration, multi-agent coordination, and model-serving infrastructure from scratch, we are migrating Data Sherpa onto Open WebUI, an actively maintained open-source platform providing local model deployment, containerized infrastructure, multi-agent workflows, and code generation. This migration runs on Jetstream2, allocated through NSF ACCESS, advancing our goal of full data sovereignty. The system's most distinguishing design goal, its ability to explicitly acknowledge uncertainty rather than produce a fluent but unsupported answer, is not yet implemented. Its conceptual design and an evaluation plan for measuring retrieval accuracy and abstention reliability are under active development, informed by the Open WebUI migration, and will be presented at the conference. Beyond the DES proof-of-concept, Data Sherpa has confirmed deployments planned with the South Pole Telescope (SPT) project, the Terahertz Intensity Mapper (TIM), and environmental and ecological datasets at the University of Illinois' Prairie Research Institute (PRI), demonstrating the framework's domain-agnostic design across projects within and beyond the Center for Astrophysical Surveys (CAPS) at NCSA.

title: Covert Digital Semantic Communication With Movable Antennas: Constellation Shaping, Spatial Optimization, and Semantic Mapping
authors: Yunfan Bai; Yuwen Qian; Hao Jiang; Yiyang Ni; Feng Shu; Jun Li; Shuning Zhang
abstract: Digital semantic communication (SemCom) is emerging as a bandwidth-efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless networks by delivering the meaning of a source over finite constellations. However, the broadcast nature of wireless channels exposes transmissions to adversarial wardens, while discrete symbols deviate from the Gaussian signaling assumed by conventional covert communication. In this paper, we propose a covert digital SemCom system assisted by movable antennas (MAs), where the constellation, the antenna positions, and the semantic transceiver are jointly designed to conceal the transmission while preserving the semantic fidelity. Specifically, the maximum covert rate against the optimal detector with unknown noise level is derived in closed-form, which reveals that the legitimate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales with the moment-matching order of the constellation and the spatial gain provided by the MA array. A Gauss-Laguerre ring constellation is then designed to raise the moment-matching order under the peak power constraints, and a covert symbol mapping with rank-to-ring assignment and scrambling is developed to carry the semantics in the ordering of the latent magnitudes. Guided by the derived semantic distortion bound, the semantic encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end through an invertible flow over the designed constellation and MA array. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme supports a higher achievable covert rate and improves the reconstruction quality by 24% compared to state-of-the-art SemCom schemes.
arxiv_comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)

title: Legitimate Reconstruction Advantage in Wiretapped Semantics-Aware Remote Monitoring
authors: Bowen Li; Nikolaos Pappas
abstract: This paper investigates joint accuracy and security in semantics-aware remote monitoring, where source updates intended for a legitimate receiver may also be intercepted by an eavesdropper. We define legitimate reconstruction advantage (LRA) as the joint event that the intended receiver correctly reconstructs the current source state using received updates while the eavesdropper reconstructs it incorrectly. Source evolution changes the relevance of received updates at the two receivers, so their marginal reconstruction accuracies do not, in general, determine the probability of this joint event. Under randomized stationary (RS) transmission and zero-order-hold reconstruction at both receivers, we derive an explicit joint stationary distribution and closed-form expressions for LRA probability and persistence for general finite-state ergodic Markov sources. For two-state and uniform-transition sources, we obtain algebraic expressions that enable low-complexity optimization of RS policies. Analytical and numerical results show that maximizing the probability of legitimate advantage need not maximize its persistence. For two-state sources, rare-transmission analysis reveals that, at a fixed sum of transition probabilities, greater transition asymmetry can increase persistence while reducing LRA probability. Moreover, optimizing marginal accuracy and security metrics can select policies that are suboptimal for LRA. Counterintuitively, more frequent transmission or improved legitimate-channel reliability can increase legitimate reconstruction accuracy while reducing LRA probability. Finally, a geofencing application translates prescribed LRA requirements into spatial constraints on eavesdropper locations.

title: Receiver-Specific Interventional Valuation of Semantic Atoms for Budget-Constrained Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Danial Dehghani; Maximilian Lübke; Friedemann Laue; Zahra Seifaei; Norman Franchi
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent semantic communication requires deciding not only how a transmitter encodes its observation, but also which resulting semantic content should be delivered to each receiver under a limited link budget. We introduce an encoder-agnostic transmitter-side framework for receiver-specific valuation of independently selectable semantic units, termed semantic atoms. Each atom is assigned a signed value that quantifies whether delivering it is expected to improve or degrade the intended receiver's downstream decision. We formulate this effect through a controlled-delivery utility and identify it via prospective randomized payload delivery before the receiver acts. A shadow receiver estimates this utility using only transmitter-available information, from which receiver-specific leave-one-out (LOO) and Shapley atom values are computed. Experiments on a four-receiver intersection benchmark show 68.4% accuracy in recovering the sign of non-negligible LOO atom effects and a Spearman correlation of 0.302 between estimated and reference LOO values. Under limited budgets, we show that receiver-specific selection consistently outperforms shared and random alternatives, demonstrating the benefit of adapting semantic ranking to the intended receiver. At full affordability, exhaustive subset selection also outperforms full-payload transmission, showing that transmitting all available content need not maximize receiver utility. Overall, our results show that receiver-specific semantic valuation can support effective budget-constrained communication despite imperfect atom-value estimation.

title: Semantic Edge-Cloud Communication for Real-Time Urban Traffic Digital Twins
authors: Murat Arda Onsu; Arman Dogru; Poonam Lohan; Burak Kantarci; Aisha Syed
abstract: Urban traffic systems are becoming increasingly complex, demanding real-time traffic perception, proactive collision prediction, and intelligent management to improve safety and reduce congestion. Although AI-driven traffic management has shown strong promise, its success relies on diverse, high-quality data spanning critical scenarios such as collisions, near-collisions, and traffic rule violations. Digital twins offer a powerful solution by enabling synchronized virtual replicas of physical traffic environments for real-time monitoring, collision prediction, traffic-flow optimization, and diverse realistic scenario generation. However, continuously synchronizing a high-fidelity urban traffic digital twin through edge surveillance cameras requires substantial edge-cloud communication, and transmitting raw video streams leads to severe bandwidth and latency constraints. To overcome this challenge, this paper proposes a semantic communication-based edge-cloud framework for real-time urban traffic digital twin applications. By leveraging edge intelligence to extract and transmit only task-relevant semantic traffic information instead of full video feeds, the proposed framework significantly reduces communication overhead while preserving the essential dynamics needed for accurate real-time digital twin reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate more than 99% transmission savings and an average trajectory reconstruction error of only 0.12 m, confirming the proposed framework as an effective, scalable, and low-latency solution for AI-enabled urban traffic digital twin applications.
arxiv_comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, accepted to IEEE Global Communications (Globecom) Conference, 2026

title: Adaptive Semantic Communication with Residual Quantization for Resilient Vehicular Networks
authors: Xuanhao Luo; Ruichen Gao; Sandeep Sreenivasan; Zhizhen Li; Yuchen Liu
abstract: Vehicular networks require timely visual information exchange to support safety-critical applications such as cooperative perception and hazard awareness, yet transmitting high-dimensional camera data over bandwidth-limited and dynamic wireless links remains challenging. In this paper, we propose an adaptive semantic communication architecture for vehicular multicast that adjusts the amount of visual information transmitted according to current channel conditions, available communication resources, and latency requirements. Specifically, the visual encoder uses residual quantization to represent each image at multiple bitrate and reconstruction-quality levels. At runtime, the system selects an appropriate level based on the communication conditions, enabling it to trade visual fidelity for lower transmission overhead when network resources are limited. Context-adaptive entropy coding further compresses the quantized representations using offline-learned statistics, without requiring retraining for different channel conditions. This design allows the visual representation to be learned offline while the communication strategy is adapted online. Experimental results demonstrate competitive rate-distortion performance at ultra-low bitrates, improved delivery reliability and deadline satisfaction across diverse vehicular scenarios, and strong downstream perception performance, achieving up to 0.88 mAP50 while dynamically adapting to changing communication conditions.

title: Cross-Domain Behavioural Mapping for IoT Attack Detection in Educational Networks Using CICIoT-2023 Dataset
authors: P Basil Raja; L Arockiam; A Aloysius
venue: Indian Journal of Science and Technology
abstract: Objectives: The study develops a cross-domain behavioural intrusion-detection framework for transferring attack knowledge from CICIoT-2023 to a derived educational IoT representation. Method: The proposed Cross-Domain Behavioural Mapping Intrusion Detection System (CDBM-IDS) integrates an Educational IoT Digital Twin Layer (E-DTL), Behaviour Spectrum Encoder (BSE), Hierarchical Deviance Encoder (HDE), Tri-Context Fusion (TCF), and Sector-Transfer Consistency Loss (STC-Loss). EduTwin is generated from CICIoT-2023 through educational device-role mapping, interaction modelling, and sector-oriented behavioural transformation. Findings: Under the controlled EduTwin evaluation protocol, CDBM-IDS achieves 98.72% accuracy, 98.64% precision, 98.51% recall, 98.57% F1-score, and 99.21% AUC-ROC. Ablation analysis confirms measurable contributions from BSE, HDE, TCF, and STC-Loss. Novelty: The framework introduces educational role abstraction, frequency-domain behavioural encoding, hierarchical deviation modelling, geometric context fusion, and consistency-driven sector mapping. Keywords: IoT security, educational network, intrusion detection, cross-domain learning, behaviour modelling

title: CONTEXT-AWARE DIGITAL TWIN ARCHITECTURES FOR REAL-TIME TRANSPORTATION AND WAREHOUSE OPTIMIZATION IN CLOUD-NATIVE SUPPLY CHAIN PLATFORMS
authors: Mahir Anwar
venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
abstract: Context-aware digital twins are emerging as enabling architectures for coordinating responses to disruptions across inventory, warehouse, and transportation operations in cloud-based supply-chain platforms. They are important because they can be used to link continually evolving operational representations with optimization services that are able to react to traffic conditions, order arrivals, equipment status, changes in inventory, and facility constraints. This article reviews peer-reviewed journal literature on digital supply-chain twins, warehouse intelligence, dynamic vehicle routing, Internet of Things-enabled logistics, microservice architectures, and computational modelling. Some studies indicate that digital-twin approaches can improve visibility, scenario evaluation, and decision coordination in specific settings, but there is very little evidence of fully integrated real-time optimization of transportation and warehouse operations. Closed-loop orchestration has not been a primary focus of existing implementations, which tend to focus on warehouse simulation or monitoring, route adjustment, or resilience analysis across logistics domains. Other limitations include insufficient semantic interoperability, inadequate model fidelity, inconsistent latency assessment, deployment evidence, and consideration of cybersecurity and human intervention. The field therefore needs architectures that integrates event-driven context management, federated twin models, scalable optimization, auditable decision services, and explicit uncertainty handling.

title: Geopolitical Risk Prediction and Robust Investment Decision-Making for Transnational Photovoltaic Projects in Africa via Generative AI and Spatiotemporal GNN
authors: Jiayu Sun; Guan Yang; Zhenguo Cao; Wei Zhao
venue: Archives des sciences a multidisciplinary journal
abstract: Geopolitical risks associated with transnational photovoltaic (PV) projects in Africa are dynamic, interconnected, and difficult to assess using conventional investment models. Specifically, existing approaches often struggle to characterize cross-border risk transmission and incorporate evolving geopolitical information into investment decisions. To address these challenges, this study proposes EG-GeoInvest, a framework that integrates generative artificial intelligence (AI) with spatiotemporal graph neural networks for geopolitical risk assessment and risk-aware investment decision-making. First, geopolitical event records, multilingual news, national governance indicators, and PV investment data are combined within an evidence-constrained, multisource heterogeneous information system to support the identification and semantic representation of risk events. Second, a Spatiotemporal Geopolitical Risk Encoding Module (ST-GREM) integrates a temporal convolutional network with relationship-aware graph convolution to represent the evolution of risks and their interdependencies across transnational investment, energy-trade, and financing networks. Third, cross-modal semantic projection and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enable graph-structured information and generative language models to contribute jointly to forecasts of geopolitical risks, project delays, and economic loss distributions. Finally, the predicted risk distributions inform a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and distributionally robust optimization framework for investment allocation under return and tail-risk constraints. A proposed evaluation design encompassing comparative risk prediction, cross-country generalization, and investment scenario analysis provides a basis for assessing predictive performance and potential decision-making value.

title: Semantic Change of Arabic Loanwords in German Across Selected Scientific Domains
authors: Selsabil Ayache; Mohamed Mohamed Yunis Ali
abstract: This research aims to examine the semantic change of Arabic loanwords in German within selected scientific domains. While scholarship on Arabic loanwords has primarily concentrated on etymology and transmission history, German as a receiving language has been comparatively understudied with respect to semantic change, especially from a domain-specific perspective. This study investigates the linguistic contact between Arabic and German, measures the extent of Arabic influence in the German scientific vocabulary, and conducts a detailed analysis of the processes of semantic change in these terms. The analysis is based on a lexicographically documented dataset of forty loanwords distributed across four scientific domains that emerged from the data. The findings reveal varied patterns of semantic change, of which broadening and narrowing are the most frequent, alongside instances of retention, while metaphorical shifts were attested in limited terms. Semantic broadening reflects the integration of terms into wider scientific contexts, whereas narrowing corresponds to the demands of precision characteristic of scientific discourse. Certain terms retained their original meanings, and metaphorical shifts emerged from cultural reinterpretation. Metonymy was absent, which affirms the nature of scientific terminology that favours standardization and stable definitions over associative meaning typical of metonymy.

title: Comparative Philology and the Historical Semiotics of Qur'anic Lexemes: An Etymological, Cross-Linguistic, and Semantic Change Study of Qur'anic Vocabulary
authors: Hamidreza Ramroudi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This study aims to develop a philological framework for the comparative study of Qur’anic lexemes in relation to other languages. It examines ten Qur’anic words—Injīl (Gospel), Firdaws (Paradise), Sakīnah (tranquility), Furqān (criterion), Ṣirāṭ (path), Qisṭās (balance or measuring instrument), Mishkāt (niche), Sijjīl (baked clay or stones of punishment), Raḥmān (the Most Merciful), and Abb (pasture or vegetation)—from historical, etymological, and semantic perspectives. Employing a descriptive-analytical approach and comparative philological methods, the study investigates the forms of these words, their Qur’anic usage, their possible cognates in Semitic, Greek, and Iranian languages, hypotheses concerning historical transmission, and processes of semantic change. Within this framework, linguistic cognacy, direct and indirect borrowing, formal similarity, and semantic development are treated as distinct phenomena. The findings indicate that the etymological status of the selected lexemes varies considerably. The historical relationship between Injīl and the Greek lexical family, as well as the connections between Firdaws and Iranian and Greek linguistic traditions, warrant further investigation. By contrast, competing hypotheses remain concerning Furqān and Sijjīl, while the origins of certain words, including Mishkāt and Abb, require more thoroughly documented examination. Furthermore, the comparison of Sakīnah and Raḥmān demonstrates that shared Semitic roots should not be conflated with direct borrowing or with the historical transmission of a religious concept. Overall, the study emphasizes the need to integrate linguistic and historical evidence with contextual analysis of the Qur’anic text and the conceptual relationships among its lexemes. Its methodological conclusion is that lexical resemblance alone is insufficient to establish a foreign origin; each etymological hypothesis must instead be evaluated against phonological, semantic, historical, and textual evidence. The study proposes a preliminary framework for developing independent, evidence-based philological dossiers for Qur’anic lexemes.

title: ZAC-Perception: Collective Provisioning of Perceptual Capabilities in Multi-Agent Embodied Intelligence
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Perception in embodied intelligent systems is commonly organized around individual agents that acquire sensor measurements, process their observations, and construct local representations of their environments. Although this architecture supports autonomy and reduces dependence on communication, it can require each agent to carry substantial sensing and computing hardware even when some perceptual capabilities could be supplied by other agents. Multi-robot collaborative perception, distributed sensor fusion, and communication-efficient feature sharing have already investigated many aspects of collective environmental understanding. However, the relationship between collective perception and the local hardware provisioning decisions of individual agents deserves explicit investigation. This paper proposes ZAC-Perception, a research framework for the collective provisioning of perceptual capabilities. Its central principle is that an individual agent need not independently provision every sensor, processing stage, or intermediate representation required by its tasks, provided that the corresponding perceptual requirements can be satisfied through eligible services supplied by other agents or shared infrastructure. Under this framework, sensing, detection, tracking, geometric reconstruction, semantic interpretation, and multi-view fusion are treated as potentially distributed services whose allocation is jointly determined with local sensor and computing configurations. The framework distinguishes physical sensor availability, observation generation, perceptual computation, information transmission, and final scene construction. It introduces a joint optimization formulation for local hardware provisioning, observation-to-node assignment, perception-stage allocation, information representation selection, communication scheduling, and reliability management. A communication-aware observation utility model is proposed to account for information gain, redundancy, freshness, uncertainty, and transmission cost. The framework also identifies conditions under which removing a local sensor or processor may be feasible, economically beneficial, or operationally unacceptable. ZAC-Perception does not claim that collaborative perception itself is new or that removing local hardware necessarily improves system performance. Rather, it establishes a testable research program centered on the joint design of collective perceptual services and minimum feasible local configurations. A proposed evaluation methodology compares individual, fixed-hardware collaborative, and jointly optimized provisioning architectures under equivalent perception requirements. The framework's scientific value ultimately depends on whether it produces measurable improvements in lifecycle cost, resource utilization, perceptual quality, communication efficiency, and resilience. Keywords: ZAC-Perception; collective provisioning; collaborative perce

title: A Lightweight Traffic Sign Recognition Network for Autonomous Driving: Integrating Dual-Branch Attention and Weather-Robust Augmentation
authors: Ting Wang; Zhihao Weng
venue: Journal of Engineering Systems and Applications
abstract: Traffic sign recognition is a key perception task in autonomous driving and advanced driver-assistance systems, where accuracy and real-time performance directly affect road safety. In real-world scenes, fog, rain, and low illumination reduce image contrast and introduce noise, degrading deep models, while in-vehicle platforms impose strict limits on model size and computation. We propose CAMSNet, a lightweight traffic sign recognition network. Its architecture uses a lightweight residual backbone based on depthwise separable convolutions and a Dual-branch Attention Calibration Module (DACM), whose parallel channel- and position-attention branches model channel dependencies and spatial location. Their weights are fused elementwise and applied through residual reweighting to enhance sign features adaptively. During training, a weather-robust augmentation strategy based on atmospheric scattering randomly adds synthetic fog, Gaussian noise, and brightness changes. This augmentation is applied only to training data, leaving inference as a lightweight, one-way network. On the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB), CAMSNet achieves 98.19% top-1 accuracy with 0.458 million parameters and 35.88 million multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), exceeding ResNet-18, which has about 24 times as many parameters, and MobileNetV2, which has about five times as many. CAMSNet with weather augmentation (CAMSNet+W) reaches 98.50% accuracy and 96.34% under severe synthetic fog. This is 36.98 percentage points above ResNet-18 and 36.12 points above CAMSNet without weather augmentation. CAMSNet+W also shows the smallest accuracy drops under severe noise and low brightness. Ablation and controlled comparisons indicate that attention improves robustness under degraded conditions while maintaining similar clean-domain accuracy. DACM is competitive with ECA and CBAM and offers a useful balance between parameter count and robustness. In this single run, weather augmentation improved robustness without an observed loss in clean-test accuracy. Robustness conclusions are based on synthetic corruptions; generalization to real adverse-weather scenes remains to be established.

title: Communication-efficient collaborative 4D mapping via federated temporal Gaussian pruning and knowledge-distilled neural radiance fields for post-disaster rescue robotics
authors: Lei Ding; Zhiying Hu; Jin Yue; Dong Li
abstract: Post-disaster rescue operations demand real-time, collaborative 4D mapping of dynamic ruins, yet severely damaged communication infrastructure and limited edge computing resources make conventional neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting impractical: they lack temporal representation, incur high transmission latency, and do not address the risks of centralizing raw sensor observations. To bridge this gap, we propose Fed-TGP-KD-NeRF, a federated collaborative mapping framework that integrates a learnable temporal latent code with multi-dimensional positional hashing and Fourier feature mapping to construct a continuous 4D dynamic Gaussian field. Adaptive pruning based on Gaussian opacity and gradient sensitivity removes redundant primitives, while a teacher-student knowledge distillation paradigm with intermediate-layer feature alignment and KL divergence compresses the model to approximately 10% of its original size. An improved federated averaging mechanism with dynamic weight adaptation (bandwidth and battery status) and periodic synchronization enables data-local collaboration by keeping raw observations on the originating robot. Experiments on the 3DAeroRelief dataset show that the proposed method achieves a PSNR of 32.58 dB, SSIM of 0.912, and real-time rendering at 35.26 FPS, while reducing per-round communication overhead to only 13.45 MB and converging in 42 rounds, outperforming the evaluated baseline methods. The framework balances reconstruction fidelity, communication efficiency, and raw-data locality; it does not claim a formal differential-privacy guarantee.

title: AGR: Agentic Generative Retrieval with Tool-Augmented Search
authors: Ming Yang; Yaqi Yin; Zhibo Wang; Xiaoze Jiang; Jingwei Zhuo; Chao Zhang; Quanzhi Zhu; Weiguo Zheng; Liang Zeng; Yunfeng Zhao; Jiaqiang Liu; Kefeng Wang; Yupeng Huang; Kaiqiao Zhan; Xuanping Li
abstract: Large-scale search and recommendation systems derive much of their retrieval quality from rich, heterogeneous features, yet existing generative retrieval (GR) methods struggle to exploit such feature ecosystems efficiently. Static feature injection either encodes all available signals or places them according to predetermined schemes, increasing serving cost and introducing irrelevant or conflicting evidence. More fundamentally, existing methods cannot adaptively determine when a feature is needed, which feature to select, or where it should influence hierarchical Semantic ID (SID) generation. We propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), a tool-augmented paradigm that interleaves SID generation with on-demand feature acquisition. Conditioned on the request and decoded SID prefix, AGR decides whether to invoke a tool, which feature to acquire, and where its observation should influence subsequent decoding, thereby steering generation toward feature-consistent SID branches. To supervise this behavior, we construct tool-augmented trajectories based on feature applicability and information gain along the SID hierarchy, and train the model through SID pretraining followed by tool-augmented fine-tuning. Experiments on an industrial dataset and three public benchmarks, together with an online A/B test, consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of AGR.

title: Real-Time Radar Semantic and Panoptic Scene Understanding
authors: Santosh Parit; Julia Hindel; Rohit Mohan; Georgi Pramatarov; Paul Newman; Daniele De Martini; Abhinav Valada
abstract: Robust scene understanding under varying environmental conditions is essential for safe autonomous driving. While cameras and LiDAR degrade in adverse weather and poor lighting, Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) spinning radar provides dependable 360° perception at extended ranges with minimal compute cost. However, real-time FMCW radar scene understanding is challenging due to complex signal returns, limited temporal resolution, and scarce annotated datasets. We introduce StreamRPS, a novel framework for streaming FMCW radar panoptic segmentation, comprising an automated label-generation pipeline via LiDAR scene completion and a real-time streaming network for semantic and panoptic segmentation. Our encoder-decoder streaming architecture comprises a radar-specific hierarchical Transformer encoder and task-specific decoders for semantic or panoptic prediction. Our encoder introduces a stem to capture range-dependent signatures, anisotropic patch embeddings to preserve angular resolution, and axial polar attention to separately model the periodic azimuth and bounded range axes. We further introduce azimuth roll rotation augmentation to simulate ego-vehicle rotation during training. Comprehensive experiments on the SAX and BOREAS datasets validate both our auto-labeling methodology and streaming segmentation network against established baselines. We outperform the strongest baseline by at least 1.4pp while processing sectors at over 400 FPS in a 4-sector streaming setting. We additionally provide manual annotations for 100 SAX radar scans, enabling independent evaluation of the entire framework.

title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing
authors: Jianqiang Xia; Han Xu; Dianxi Shi
abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
authors: Milad Rostamian; Mohammadreza Mohammadi; Mohsen Soryani
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

title: LaMER: Language-Conditioned Multi-Expert Routing for Weakly Supervised Referring Expression Comprehension
authors: Yu Yu Chang; Tzu-Hsuan Weng; Youssef Mohamed Amin; Mohaned Ahmed Elsayed; Hung-Hsuan Chen; Min-Te Sun; Sherine Shawky
abstract: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes the image region described by a natural language expression, underpinning applications such as autonomous navigation, human-robot interaction, and medical image analysis. Under weak supervision, REC is challenged by the visual-linguistic semantic gap and the difficulty of inferring region-text correspondences from coarse image-level signals alone. Moreover, no single visual encoder captures all complementary properties---semantic alignment, fine-grained texture, and boundary awareness---while naively fusing multiple pretrained encoders yields heterogeneous, hard-to-reconcile representations. We propose LaMER, a weakly supervised REC framework that dynamically aggregates four frozen expert encoders through a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, adapting expert selection to each referring expression without instance-level bounding-box supervision. A Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation, trained with a multi-objective loss combining contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing terms, further stabilizes optimization. LaMER achieves 77.67\%, 62.81\%, and 69.49\% Acc@IoU\(\geq 0.5\) on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, surpassing DViN and WeakMCN by up to 16.49 and 14.49 points, with ablations validating each component.

title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
authors: Marwan Farag; Bin Yang
abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.

title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
authors: Jonathan Leung; Zhiqi Shen; Deheng Ye
abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.

title: SAPO: Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization for Improving Temporal Video Grounding in Vision-Language Models
authors: Zixuan Chen; Depeng Wang; Wei Chen; Ke Xu; Ya Guo; Huijia Zhu; Tanfeng Sun; Xinghao Jiang
abstract: Video vision-language models (VLMs) have strong semantic understanding, yet remain unreliable at precise temporal grounding. Existing gains from explicitly aligning video frames with absolute time suggest that VLMs may already encode accurate temporal locations internally but lose precision when expressing them as timestamps. Our analysis across four VLMs and two grounding datasets confirms this hypothesis: attention intervals outperform predicted intervals on approximately 66% of valid examples. We term this discrepancy the temporal generation gap. Because precise temporal annotations are expensive, this finding motivates closing the gap to improve temporal grounding using only unlabeled video-query pairs. We propose Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses internal temporal attention as self-supervision for Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value samples. SAPO consistently improves temporal grounding across multiple datasets and models spanning weak to strong initial grounding ability. Relative mIoU gains reach 33.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 5.4% on the strong Time-R1-7B. The improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.

title: HyperTaxa: Multiscale Genome Representations for Generalized Microbial Taxonomic Inference
authors: Akash Rao; Sushim Gupta; Vishalini Ramnath; Akhilesh Ramachandran; Sathyanarayanan Aakur
abstract: Reliable microbial taxonomic inference is challenged by the rapid growth of newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. While alignment- and database-driven tools remain essential for reference-backed identification, they are not designed for learned inference over species absent from genome-level training. We introduce HyperTaxa, a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework for open-set microbial taxonomic inference. HyperTaxa encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns these representations to a taxonomy-derived semantic space using a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure that combines local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. The resulting space supports zero-shot inference over species excluded from genome-level training but represented in the taxonomy, generalized zero-shot inference over seen and unseen species, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa improves taxonomic prediction over pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the strongest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations further show that multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment are key contributors to generalization. These results position HyperTaxa as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.

title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Hayat; Jahangir Baig; Shayan Ahmed; Ahmed Faraz Ayubi
abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

title: Agentic code modernization
authors: Peter F. Peterson; Addi Malviya Thakur
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Software rots. Between refactors for new features, bug fixes, the continual march of cybersecurity advisories, and the slow drift of dependencies toward end-of-life, code must change or cease to exist. The simple act of keeping up can be overwhelming for research software engineers tasked with maintaining long-lived scientific codebases. To address this maintenance burden, the community has developed a vibrant ecosystem of language- and framework-specific tools, such as Dependabot for dependency bumps [1], Clang-Tidy for C++ static analysis [2], and Python Refurb for idiom modernization [3], alongside a host of similar utilities. These tools, while monumental in their contribution, are necessarily limited in scope: they encode a fixed catalog of transformations, they tend to operate on a single file or a single dependency at a time, and they presumably cannot reason about the broader architectural or semantic consequences of a change. More recently, agentic AI systems have arrived. Unlike single-shot code completion, agentic systems can read across a repository, run tests, observe failures, and iterate, and these behaviors, in principle, may enable a different class of modernization task. In this talk, we present concrete examples of modernizing Mantid [4], a more than 20-year-old C++ and Python project with roughly two million lines of code. We attempted to leverage agentic AI to perform maintenance work and modernization work on research software. Changes proposed by the agents were validated against the project's existing automated test suite and reviewed by human maintainers before merging. By exploring successes and failures, the presentation will improve attendees' understanding of when, and with what guardrails, to use AI to assist in modernizing their code. References Dependabot.
